(p-524) Surah al-Furqan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed﴾ (tabaraka) is of the form tafā'ala from al-barakah (blessing), which is abundance of good and its increase. The meaning of "tabāraka Allāh" is that His good increases and multiplies, or that He is exalted above everything in His attributes and actions. It is a word of glorification that is used only for Allah alone, and the only form of it that is used is the past tense (al-māḍī) and nothing else.

﴿Who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqān)﴾. Al-Furqān is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn, meaning to separate between two things when one divides them. The Qur'an is named by this because it separates between truth and falsehood and between the lawful and the unlawful. Or it is because it was not sent down all at once, but in portions, with parts separated from one another in the revelation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And a Qur'an which We have divided (farraqnāhu) so that you may recite it to the people at intervals, and We have sent it down in gradual revelation﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:106].

﴿To His servant﴾, Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. ﴿That he may be﴾ — the servant or the Criterion — ﴿a warner to the worlds﴾, to the jinn and mankind. The universality of the message is among the distinctive features of him, upon him be prayers and peace.

﴿A warner (nadhīran)﴾: i.e., one who warns, frightening; or a warning, like nakīr in the sense of inkār (denial). From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings (nudhur)?﴾ [al-Qamar 54:18].

﴿Alladhi﴾ (the one who) is in the nominative case, either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿alladhi nazzala﴾ (He who sent down). It is also permissible to separate the substitute from the word it replaces by the phrase ﴿li-yakūna﴾ (so that it may be), because the substituted word's relative clause is ﴿nazzala﴾ (sent down), and ﴿li-yakūna﴾ gives the reason for that. It is as if the word being replaced was not complete without it. Alternatively, ﴿alladhi﴾ may be in the accusative case as an expression of praise (*madh*), meaning "I praise Him who..." ﴿Lahu mulku al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ﴾ (To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth) in an absolute sense. ﴿Wa-lam yattakhidh waladan﴾ (and He has not taken a son), as the Jews said of ʿUzayr and the Christians said of al-Masīḥ, peace be upon them both. ﴿Wa-lam yakun lahu sharīkun fi al-mulk﴾ (and He has no partner in the dominion) (p-525), as the Thanawiyya (Dualists) claimed. ﴿Wa-khalaqa kulla shayʾin﴾ (and He created everything): that is, He brought every thing into existence alone, not as the Magians and the Dualists say, with light and darkness, "Yazdān and Ahrimān." There is no ambiguity in this for those who say that God is a "thing," nor for those who hold that the Qur'an is created, because the agent (*fāʿil*) in all his attributes cannot be an object (*mafʿūl*) of this kind. Moreover, the word *shayʾ* (thing) is restricted to that which can be created, by the contextual indicator of ﴿wa-khalaqa﴾. This is the clearest proof for us against the Muʿtazila regarding the creation of human acts. ﴿Fa-qaddarahu taqdīran﴾ (and then He determined it precisely): that is, He prepared it for what suits it without any defect in it, just as He created man in this form that you see, and determined him for the obligations and interests bound to him in religion and in this world. Or it means He determined it to endure until a known term.

Surah 25, verse 3: "And they have taken, besides Him, gods (ʾālihah) that create nothing, while they themselves are created..."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil):

﴿وَاتَّخَذُوا﴾ "And they have taken": the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, because they are included under "the worlds" (al-ʿālamīn), or because the word "warner" (nadhīran) in the preceding verse points to them, since they are the ones being warned. ﴿مِن دُونِهِ آلِهَةً﴾ "besides Him, gods," that is, the idols. ﴿لا يَخْلُقُونَ شَيْئًا وهم يُخْلَقُونَ﴾ "that create nothing, while they themselves are created." That is: they preferred to worship, over the One who alone possesses divinity (al-ulūhiyyah), sovereignty, creation and decree, the worship of impotent beings who are unable to create anything while they themselves are created. ﴿وَلا يَمْلِكُونَ لأنْفُسِهِمْ ضَرًّا ولا نَفْعًا﴾ "And they have no power over harm or benefit for themselves": they cannot repel harm from themselves or bring benefit to themselves. ﴿وَلا يَمْلِكُونَ مَوْتًا﴾ "Nor do they have power over death," meaning causing death (ʾimātah), ﴿وَلا حَياةً﴾ "nor life," meaning giving life (ʾiḥyāʾ), ﴿وَلا نُشُورًا﴾ "nor resurrection," meaning giving life after death. He treated them as if they were rational beings, according to the claim of their worshippers.

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "This is not﴾ (i.e., what is this Qur'an?) ﴿except a fabrication﴾ (i.e., a lie) ﴿that he has invented﴾ (i.e., he himself fabricated and originated it, Muhammad, from his own self) ﴿and others helped him with it﴾ (i.e., the Jews, Addas, Yasar, and Abu Fukayha al-Rumi). This was said by al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. ﴿Then they have produced injustice and falsehood﴾ (ﷺ). This is information from Allah, a refutation of the disbelievers. So the pronoun (ḍamīr) returns to the disbelievers. The verb "جاءَ" (jāʾa, "to come") is used in the sense of "فَعَلَ" (faʿala, "to do"), so it takes its object directly. Or the preposition is omitted and the verb reaches its object directly, meaning: with injustice and falsehood. Their injustice is that they made the Arab (al-ʿarabī) learn from the non-Arab Roman (al-ʿajamī al-rūmī) speech in Arabic that outdid all the eloquent Arabs in its eloquence. The falsehood (al-zūr) is that they slandered him by attributing to him what he is innocent of.

﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients."﴾ Or it is "the stories of the earlier people" and what they wrote down, like Rustum and others. It is the plural of *asṭār* (lines, sing. *saṭr*), and *usṭūra* (*asāṭīr*, "tale," singular) follows the pattern of *uḥdūtha* (a story). ﴿He had it written down﴾: he wrote them for himself. ﴿So they are dictated to him﴾: i.e., they are recited to him from his book, ﴿in the morning﴾: at the beginning of the day, ﴿and in the evening﴾: at its end. So he memorises what is dictated to him, then recites it to us.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 6:

﴿Say﴾ O Muhammad, ﴿"He has sent it down"﴾ — i.e., the Qur'an — ﴿"He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth."﴾ That is: He knows every secret that is hidden in the heavens and the earth. The meaning is that since the Qur'an includes knowledge of the unseen matters which it is normally impossible for Muhammad (peace be upon him) to know without being taught, this indicates that it comes from the Knower of the unseen. ﴿"Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ So He gives them respite and does not hasten to punish them, even though they deserve it for their obstinate opposition to him.

And they said, ﴿"What is the matter with this Messenger?"﴾ The letter lām in مَالِ was written in the mushaf (the codified text of the Qur'an) separated from the hā' of هَذا, and the orthography of the mushaf is a sunnah (an established practice) that may not be changed. Their calling him "the Messenger" is mockery on their part, as if they had said, "What is this claimant who asserts that he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?"

﴿Who eats food and walks in the markets﴾ is a ḥāl (a circumstantial qualifier, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), and its governing element (ʿāmil) is هَذا ("this"). ﴿Why has no angel been sent down to him, so that he might be a warner together with him?﴾

﴿Or a treasure is thrown down to him, or he has a garden from which he eats.﴾ That is: if it is true that he is the Messenger of God, then what is the matter with him that he eats food as we eat, and walks about in the markets seeking a livelihood as we walk about? They mean that he should have been an angel, free from the need to eat and to earn a living. Then they came down from that proposal to his being a human being accompanied by an angel, so that the two would support one another in warning and frightening. Then they came down further to his being given a treasure cast down to him from heaven, which he would use as support and would not need to seek a livelihood. Then they came down to his being a man who has a garden, from which he eats, like the wealthy, or from which we eat. [p. 527] As in the qira'a (recitation) of Ali and Hamza, the verb ﴿yulqā﴾ is coordinated with the present tense ﴿takūnu﴾, and ﴿takūnu﴾ is coordinated with ﴿unzila﴾, which is in the past tense, because the present tense is attached to it. The verb ﴿fa-yakūna﴾ in the well-known recitation is in the accusative, because it is the answer to ﴿lawlā﴾ in the sense of ﴿halla﴾ (why not), and its ruling is the ruling of an interrogative. By ﴿al-ẓālimīn﴾ (the wrongdoers) in the phrase ﴿and the wrongdoers said﴾ he means the same people, but he placed the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, to record upon them the wrong in what they said. They were the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿You follow none but a man bewitched﴾: bewitched, so he has become mad, or one who has suffered sorcery, which is the lung. They meant that he is a human being and not an angel.

Look how they coined comparisons for you (﴿انْظُرْ كَيْفَ ضَرَبُوا﴾). Al-Amthal (الأمثال) means the likenesses, i.e., the similitudes. They said those sayings about you and invented for you the attributes and conditions: a fabricator (المُفْتَرِي), one who has things dictated to him (المُمْلى عَلَيْهِ), and one who is bewitched (المَسْحُورِ). ﴿فَضَلُّوا﴾ they went astray from the truth, ﴿فَلا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ سَبِيلا﴾ so they cannot find a way to it, meaning they do not find a path leading to it.

Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces.

That is: abundant in good is the One who, if He wills, bestows upon you in this world something better than what they said, namely that He hastens for you the like of what He has promised you in the Hereafter of gardens and palaces. "Gardens" (jannat) is a substitute (badal) for "better" (khayran).

"And He will give" (wa yaj'al) with the nominative (raf') is read by Makki, Shami and Abu Bakr, because when the conditional (shart) occurs in the past tense, its response (jaza') may be in the jussive (jazm) or the nominative (raf').

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 11:

﴿Nay, they denied the Hour﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what was related about them. It means: "Nay, they came with something more wondrous than all that, namely their denial of the Hour." Or it is connected to what follows it, as if he said: "Nay, they denied the Hour. So how would they turn to this reply, and how would they believe in the hastening of the like of what He promised you in the Hereafter, when they do not believe in it?" ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blazing Fire﴾ And We have readied for those who deny it a fierce fire, in the sense of [the word] istiʿar (blazing).

﴿When it sees them﴾, i.e., the Fire, i.e., it confronts them, ﴿from a distant place﴾, i.e., when it is in their sight from afar, the onlookers at a distance, ﴿they will hear from it raging and roaring﴾, i.e., they will hear the sound of its seething, and this was likened to the sound of one who rages and roars. Or: when its guardians see them, they rage and roar in anger at the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 13:

﴿And when they are thrown into it﴾ from the Fire, ﴿into a narrow place﴾. "ḍayyiqan" (narrow) is read by Makki with the "ḍ" vowelled as a short "ḍayqan" [i.e., ḍayqan, with the sukun variant]: distress accompanies narrowness just as ease accompanies spaciousness. For this reason Paradise is described as having a breadth of "the heavens and the earth." It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that it (the Fire) constricts them just as the butt-spike (zajj) constricts within the spear.

﴿Bound together﴾ means: along with that narrowness they are chained and linked in shackles; their hands are tied to their necks in the fetters. Or, each disbeliever is bound together with his devil in one chain. And on their feet are the shackles.

﴿They will call out there﴾ at that time ﴿for destruction﴾, i.e., ruin. They will say: "Woe to us!" That is, "Come, O destruction, for this is your time." Then it will be said to them:
﴿Do not call out for one destruction today, but call out for many destructions.﴾ That is: you have fallen into a state in which your destruction is not a single one; rather, it is many destructions.

Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of eternity which the God-fearing have been promised?" That is, the aforementioned description of the Fire is better, or the Garden of eternity which the God-fearing have been promised. That is: which they have been promised. So the returning pronoun to the relative (al-ladhi) is omitted. He said "Is that better?" regarding the Fire only as a rebuke to the disbelievers. ﴿It shall be for them a recompense﴾, a reward, ﴿and a destination﴾, a place of return. It was said "it shall be" (kanat) because what Allah promises is, as it were, already existent on account of its certainty; or that it was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh, the Tablet) before He created them.

﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾, i.e., whatever they desire (مَا يَشَاءُونَهُ). ﴿Abiding eternally﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a grammatical term for a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) referring to the pronoun in يَشَاءُونَ. The pronoun in ﴿كَانَ﴾ refers to ما يشاءون. ﴿It is for your Lord a promise﴾, i.e., a promised thing (مَوْعُودًا), ﴿to be asked for﴾, i.e., something sought (مَطْلُوبًا), or something worthy of being asked for (حَقِيقًا أَنْ يُسْأَلَ), or something the Muslims and the angels have already asked for in their supplications: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 194]; ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201]; ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You have promised them﴾ [Ghāfir: 8] (p-529).

"And the Day We gather them" (for the resurrection, al-ba'th, according to the majority of scholars). Makki, Yazid, Ya'qub and Hafs read it with the ya' (يَحْشُرُهم).

﴿And what they worship besides God﴾ means the worshipped ones among the angels, the Messiah and 'Uzayr (Ezra). From al-Kalbi: it means the idols, which God will give speech. It was also said that the term is general. The word "ma" (ما) includes rational beings and others, because it is intended as a description, as if it were said: "and their worshipped ones."

﴿Then He will say﴾ is read with the nun (فَيَقُولُ نَحْنُ) by al-Shami (Ibn 'Amir).

﴿Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?﴾

The analogical form would be ضَلُّوا عَنِ السَبِيلِ (they strayed from the way), but they omitted the preposition, as they omitted it in هَداهُ الطَرِيقَ (he guided him to the way). The original is إلى الطَرِيقِ or لِلطَّرِيقِ. ضَلَّ is the intransitive counterpart (mutawi') of أضَلَّهُ (to cause someone to go astray).

The meaning: "Did you bring them into straying from the path of truth by introducing doubts, or did they stray from it by themselves?"

Why it does not say أأضْلَلْتُمْ عِبادِي هَؤُلاءِ أمْ ضَلُّوا السَبِيلَ, but adds "you" (أنْتُمْ) and "they" (هُمْ): the question is not about the act itself and its existence, for without its existence this reproach would not arise. It is about the one who performed it, so he must be mentioned and placed after the interrogative particle, so that it is known that he is the one being asked about. The benefit of asking them, although He, exalted is He, knows who is being asked about, is that they answer as they answered, so that He rebukes their worshippers by their denial of them, and their regret increases.

**"They will say, 'Glory be to You!'"** This is an expression of their amazement at what was said to them. By it they meant to declare Him free of having rivals, and free of having a prophet, an angel, or anything else be His equal.

**"It was not for us to take any allies apart from You."** That is, it was not right or proper for us to take anyone other than You as a protector. So how could it be right for us to cause others to take us as protectors instead of You?

**"Nattakhidha"** is read by Yazid. The verb *ittakhadha* (to take) is transitive to one object, as in *ittakhadha waliyyan* (he took a friend), and transitive to two objects, as in *ittakhadhna fulanan waliyyan* (we took so-and-so as a friend). God, may He be exalted, says: **"Or have they taken gods from the earth?"** [al-Anbiya: 21] (p. 530) and He says: **"And God took Abraham as an intimate friend."** [al-Nisa: 125]. So the first reading (*nattakhidha*) is transitive to one object, which is **"min awliya'"** (from among allies). The underlying form is *an nattakhidha awliya'*, and *min* was added to emphasize the sense of negation. The second reading (*nattakhidha*, in the form with two objects) is transitive to two objects: the first object is the one the verb is built upon (the implied subject of the passive form, i.e., "us"), and the second is **"min awliya'"**. Here *min* is partitive, meaning: we would not take *some* of the allies. This is because *min* is not added to the second object; rather, it is added to the first. You say *ma ittakhadhtu min ahadin waliyyan* (I did not take any of the people as a friend), and you do not say *ma ittakhadhtu ahadan min waliyyin* (I did not take anyone from among friends).

**"But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment"** through wealth, children, long life, and safety from punishment.

**"Until they forgot the remembrance"**, that is, the remembrance of God, belief in Him, the Qur'an, and the laws (*shara'i'*).

**"And they were"** before God **"a people ruined"**, that is, destroyed. *Bur* is the plural of *ba'ir*, like *ta'idh* and *'udh*.

Then the unbelievers are addressed directly, by way of a shift from the third person (absence) to the second person (address): [the verse continues in the following part of the commentary].

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 25, verse 19:**

﴿Then they have indeed denied you﴾. This sudden address (al-mufaja'at) through argument and binding proof (al-ihtijaj wal-ilzam) is excellent and striking, especially when it is combined with *al-iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person, such as from third person to second person) and *hadhf al-qawl* (omitting the verb "to say"). A parallel to it is ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you [the message] after a interval [of no messengers]﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19], up to His saying ﴿there has certainly come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. Also the saying of the poet:

*They said: "Khurasan is the farthest that we are wanted for, then the return."*
*So we have indeed come to Khurasan.*

﴿with what you say﴾: with your saying about them that they are gods. The *ba'* (بِ) in this reading is like His saying ﴿Nay, they denied the truth﴾ [Qaf: 5]. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wal-majrur) is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, as if it were said: "They have denied what you say." It is also reported from Qunbul, with the *ya'* (يَ), that the meaning is: "They have denied you by their saying, 'Glory be to You, it was not for us to take any protectors besides You' [al-Furqan: 18]." The *ba'* in this reading is like your saying "I wrote with the pen."

﴿So you cannot avert [the punishment] nor obtain help﴾: that is, so your gods cannot avert the punishment from you or help you. Hafs reads it with *ta'* (تَ), meaning: so you yourselves, O disbelievers, cannot avert the punishment from yourselves nor help yourselves. Then He addressed the responsible people in general with His saying ﴿And whoever among you wrongs﴾: that is, associates others with Allah in worship, because *zulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place, and whoever makes the created thing a partner of its Creator has wronged. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. ﴿We will make him taste a great punishment﴾ has been explained as eternal abiding in the Fire, and this is fitting for the polytheist but not for the sinner, except according to the view of the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij.

Al-Nasafi's commentary (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 25, verse 20:

﴿And We did not send before you any of the messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ The particle **إنَّ** (*inna*) is given a kasra (*kasrat*) because of the lam (**اللامِ**) in the predicate. The clause after **إلّا** (*illa*) is a qualifier (**صِفَةٌ**) of an omitted noun. The meaning is: "We did not send before you any messenger except that they ate and walked." The noun was omitted because the prepositional phrase **مِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ** ("of the messengers") is sufficient to indicate it. Its meaning is: "We did not send before you anyone of the messengers except that they ate and walked." A similar construction is ﴿And there is none of us except that he has a known station﴾ (al-Saffat: 164), meaning "there is none of us except that he is one who has a known station." It is said that this verse is an argument against those who said ﴿What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ (al-Furqan: 7), and a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), upon whom be peace.

﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾, meaning a test and an affliction. This is an exhortation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to be patient regarding what they reproached him for, namely poverty and his walking in the markets. The meaning is: He has made the wealthy a trial for the poor, so He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills. ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ with this trial, so that you are rewarded, or will you not be patient, so that your grief increases?

It is related that one of the righteous became weary of the hardship of his life and went out distressed. He saw a eunuch (**خصيًّا**) in processions and on mounts, and something occurred to his mind. Then he heard someone reciting this verse, so he said, "Yes, then patience, our Lord." Or the meaning is: We made you a trial for them, because if you had been wealthy, the possessor of treasures and gardens, their obedience to you would have been for the sake of this world, or mixed with worldly motives. Therefore We sent you poor, so that the obedience of those who obey you would be sincerely for Us. ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾, meaning knowing what is right in what He tests with, or knowing who is patient and who is impatient.

(p-532)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 21:

﴿And those who do not expect﴾ (lā yarjūna) meeting ﴿Us﴾ (liqā'anā): lā yaʾmulūna (they do not hope) for good; this is because they are disbelievers who do not believe in the Resurrection, or they do not fear Our punishment. Alternatively, because the one who hopes is anxious about what he hopes for, like the one who fears; or because raja' (hope) in the dialect of Tihama means fear. ﴿Why not?﴾ (lawlā) hallā (why not) ﴿have the angels been sent down to us﴾ as messengers instead of human beings, or as witnesses to his prophethood and his claim of messengership; ﴿or we see our Lord﴾ openly, so that He would inform us of his messengership and that we should follow him. ﴿Indeed they have become arrogant within themselves﴾, i.e., they concealed arrogance towards the truth, which is disbelief and obstinacy, in their hearts. ﴿And they have transgressed﴾ and exceeded the limit in wrongdoing ﴿with a great transgression﴾. He described the transgression as great, thereby emphasising its extremity; i.e., they did not dare to make this grave statement except that they had reached the utmost point of arrogance and the furthest limit of transgression. The lām in ﴿la-qad﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath.

﴿On the Day they see the angels﴾, meaning the Day of death or the Day of Resurrection. *Yawma* (يَوْمَ) is in the accusative (*mansub*) and is governed by what is implied in ﴿no good tidings﴾, meaning: on the Day they see the angels, they will be denied good tidings. His words ﴿on that day﴾ (يَوْمَئِذٍ) are an emphatic repetition of *yawma yarawna* (يَوْمَ يَرَوْنَ), or they are governed by an implied *udhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"), meaning: remember the Day they see the angels. Then He informed, saying ﴿no good tidings﴾ of Paradise on that day. It is not governed by *yarawna* (يَرَوْنَ), because the *mudaf ilayhi* (the noun in the genitive after an construct phrase) does not govern the *mudaf* (the first noun of the construct phrase). Nor is it governed by *bushra* (بُشْرى), because it is a *masdar* (verbal noun), and a *masdar* does not govern what precedes it. Also, the negated word after *la* (لا) does not govern what comes before *la*. ﴿For the guilty﴾ (لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ) is an apparent noun in place of a pronoun, or a general term that includes them by its generality. They are those who committed sins, and the intended meaning is the disbelievers, because unrestricted nouns encompass the most complete of what they designate. ﴿And they will say﴾, meaning the angels, ﴿"A forbidden barrier"﴾ (حِجْرًا مَحْجُورًا): forbidden, prohibited upon you, the good tidings. That is, God made this forbidden for you; good tidings are only for the believers. *Hijr* (حِجْرٌ) is a *masdar*. The kasra and fatha (the vowel forms *hijr* and *hajr*) are two dialects, and it has been read with both. It derives from *hajarahu* (حَجَرَهُ), when he prevented him. It is among the *masdar*s in the accusative governed by verbs whose display is omitted. *Mahjuran* (مَحْجُورًا) is for emphasizing the meaning of *hijr*, as they say *mawtun ma'it* (مَوْتٌ مائِتٌ, "a dead death").

(p-533)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 23:

﴿And We shall turn to the deeds they did, and make them scattered dust.﴾ "Qadima" here is a figure of speech (sifah); there is no actual coming (qudum) in it. Rather, the state of these people and the deeds they performed in their disbelief, such as maintaining family ties (silat rahim), relieving the distressed (ighathat malhuf), hospitality to guests (qira dayf), and the like, have been likened to the state of one who opposes a king's authority and disobeys him, so that he comes upon his possessions and makes for what is under his hands, then spoils them and tears them to every shred, leaving no trace of them. Al-haba' (the fine dust) is what comes out of a window (kuwwa) together with the light of the sun, resembling dust. Al-mansur (scattered) means dispersed. This is a metaphor (isti'arah) for rendering them into a state where they cannot be gathered together and no benefit can be derived from them.

Then He explained the superiority of the people of Paradise over the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that day are better in dwelling-place﴾. "Better" is a tamyiz (specification of comparison). The mustaqarr (dwelling-place) is the place where they remain for most of their time, sitting together and conversing. ﴿And better in resting-place﴾: a place to which they retreat for repose (istirwah) with their spouses. There is no sleep in Paradise, but the place of their rest with the houris is called a maqil (resting-place at midday) by way of metaphor. It is related that the reckoning will be concluded in the middle of that day, so the people of Paradise will take their midday rest in Paradise, and the people of the Fire in the Fire. The wording "the better" (al-ahsan) contains a mockery (tahakkum) of them.

Translation:

﴿And [remember] the day﴾ meaning: remember the day ﴿when the heaven will be split asunder﴾. The original form is "tatashaqqaqu," and the taa' was elided. Al-Kufiyyun (the Kufan readers) and Abu 'Amr read it this way, while others assimilated it into the shin (idgham). ﴿With the clouds﴾: since the splitting of the heaven occurs because of the emergence of clouds from it, he made the clouds as though they were that by which the heaven is split, just as you say, "I split the hump with the knife, so it was split by it."

﴿And the angels will be sent down, a descent﴾: "wa-nunzilu" is read by Makki, and ﴿tanzilan﴾ in this reading is a verbal noun (masdar) not from the verb's own form. The meaning is: the heaven will be opened with a white cloud coming out of it, and in the clouds the angels will descend, with the scrolls of the deeds of the servants in their hands.

Note on terms: "idgham" (assimilation of one consonant into another), "masdar" (verbal noun), and "Kufiyyun" (the Kufan school of Qur'anic readers) are technical terms used here.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 26:

﴿Al-mulk﴾ (the sovereignty) is the subject (mubtada') of the sentence; ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day) is its adverbial complement (zarf); ﴿al-haqq﴾ (the true, the real) is its attribute (na't), and its meaning is "the established, the enduring" (al-thabit), because every sovereignty passes away on that Day, so none remains except His sovereignty. ﴿Lil-Rahman﴾ (belongs to the Most Merciful) is its predicate (khabar). ﴿Wa kana﴾ (and it was) that Day ﴿yawman ʿala al-kafirin ʿasiran﴾ (a difficult day for the disbelievers), meaning severe. It is said ʿasura ʿalayhi, so he is ʿasir and ʿasir (hard for him). From this is understood its ease for the believers. Thus in the hadith: "The Day of Resurrection will be made light for the believers, until it will be lighter for them than an obligatory prayer which they prayed in the world." (ﷺ)

Biting of the hands is a metaphor (kinayah) for rage and regret, because it is among its concomitants (radifah). So the concomitant is mentioned and it points to what is concomitated (al-mardif), and the speech is thereby elevated in the level of eloquence, and the listener finds in his soul from its awe what he does not find in the wording of the thing it stands for. The definite article in "al-zalim" is for prior reference (li-l-ahd), and by it is meant ʿUqbah, as has been clarified; or it is for the class (li-l-jins), and then it includes ʿUqbah and other disbelievers. ﴿He will say: "Oh, would that I had taken﴾ in the world ﴿a way with the Messenger﴾ Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, ﴿a path﴾, a way to salvation and Paradise, which is faith.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 28:

﴿Woe to me!﴾ It is also read "Yā wailatī" with a yā' (ي) at the end, and this is the original form, because a man calls out his wailah (ويلة), which is his destruction, saying to it: "Come, for this is your time." The yā' was changed to an alif as in ṣaḥārā (صحارى, "deserts") and mudārā (مدارى, "appeasing"). ﴿Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend (khalīl)﴾. "So-and-so" (فلان, fulān) is a kināyah (metonymic substitute) for proper names. If by "the wrongdoer" is meant ʿUqbah, then this is because it has been narrated that he prepared a feast and invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but he refused to eat of his food until he pronounced the two testimonies (shahādatayn). He did so, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who was his close friend, said to him: "My face is forbidden to your face unless you turn back," so he apostatized. The meaning then is: "Would that I had not taken Ubayy as a close friend," and so he substituted a kināyah for his name. If, however, the word is taken generically, then everyone who takes one of the misguiders as a close friend has, undoubtedly, a proper name for his friend, so it is made a kināyah for him. It was also said: it is a kināyah for Satan.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 29:

﴿Indeed, he led me astray from the Reminder﴾ — that is, from the remembrance of God, or the Qur'an, or faith — ﴿after it had come to me﴾ from God. ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter to man﴾ — that is, his close friend (khalil). He named him "Satan" (shaytan) (p-535) because he led him astray the way Satan, or Iblis, leads people astray, since it was he who induced him to take as a friend the one who misleads and to oppose the Messenger. ﴿To man﴾ who obeys him. ﴿Deserter (khadhul)﴾ is an intensive form from abandonment (al-khidhlan), meaning: it is his habit to abandon the one who allies with him. This is a recounting of the words of God, or the words of the wrongdoer.

"And the Messenger says" — that is, Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, in the world — "O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned" — mahjur, meaning abandoned, left aside; that is, they abandoned it and did not believe in it, from al-hijran (forsaking). It is the second object of ittakhadhu (they have taken). In this there is an emphasis on the complaint and a warning to his people, because when prophets complain to Him about their people, punishment befalls them without delay. Then He turned to him, consoling him and promising him victory over them, so He said:

Thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals; and your Lord suffices as a guide and a helper. (Qur'an 25:31)

That is: just as every prophet before you was afflicted with the enmity of his people, so too your Lord suffices you as a guide to the path of subduing them and taking vengeance upon them, and as a helper for you against them. The word ʿaduww (enemy) may be singular or plural. The bāʾ (in bi-Rabbika) is superfluous (zāʾida), meaning: "and your Lord suffices," and hādiyan (guide) is a tamyīz (specification of the sense).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 32:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, i.e., Quraysh or the Jews: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ The word *jumlatan* is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the Qur'an, meaning gathered together. ﴿In one piece﴾ means: why was it not sent down to him in one single installment, at one time, as the (earlier) Books were sent down, and why was it sent down in parts? This is superfluous speech and disputation about something without benefit, because the matter of inimitability (i'jāz) (the miraculous inimitability of the Qur'an, as proof of prophethood) does not differ whether it is sent down all at once or in parts. Here *nuzzila* is used in the sense of *unzila*; otherwise it would be contradictory with the evidence of *jumlatan wāḥidatan*. This objection is invalid, because they were challenged to produce a single sura, from the shortest of the suras, and they exposed the page of their incapacity, until they took refuge in open opposition, resorted to war, expended their lives, and inclined to arguments. ﴿Thus﴾ is an answer to them, meaning: thus it was sent down in parts over twenty years, or over twenty-three years. The word *kadhālika* is an indication toward the implied meaning of His words ﴿why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾, because its meaning is: why was the Qur'an sent down to you in parts? So He informed them that this is ﴿so that We may strengthen thereby﴾ through its being in parts ﴿your heart﴾, so that you may comprehend it and memorize it, because the recipient's heart is only able to hold knowledge little by little, part after part; if it were cast upon him all at once, he would be unable to retain it. Or (it means) ﴿so that We may strengthen thereby your heart﴾ against impatience through the continuous arrival (of revelation) and the successive coming of the Messenger, because the heart of the lover is calmed by the continuous letters of the beloved. ﴿And We have recited it in a measured recitation﴾ is conjoined to the verb to which *kadhālika* is attached, as if He said: thus We divided it and We recited it, i.e., read it with deliberation and steadiness, or We explained it with explanation. *Tartīl* is explanation in a deliberate and steady manner.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 33:

﴿And they will not bring you any example﴾, meaning, any strange question among their false questions, as if it were itself an example of falsehood. ﴿But We bring you the truth﴾, meaning, We bring you the true answer, from which there is no escape. ﴿And better in explanation﴾, meaning, and something better in meaning and in what it conveys than their example, that is, than their question. The phrase "from their example" was omitted because the context points to it, just as when you say, "I saw Zayd and 'Amr," though 'Amr is the better one in appearance, the sentence indicates that you mean "from Zayd." Since tafsir (explanation, exposition) is the uncovering of what the speech indicates, it was used in place of its meaning, so they say, "The tafsir of this speech is such-and-such," just as it is said, "its meaning is such-and-such."

Or the meaning is: they will not bring you any strange condition or description, such as saying, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Except that We give you of the conditions what, in Our wisdom, you deserve to be given. ﴿And better in uncovering﴾ what you were sent with, and in proof of its soundness. That is, its being sent down in parts, and the challenge (tahaddi) to them to bring something like those parts each time a portion of it is revealed, is more effective in demonstrating inimitability (i'jaz) than if it were all sent down at once.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 25, verse 34:

﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell—those are worse in place and further astray in way.﴾

*Alladhina* (those who) is the *mubtada'* (the subject of a nominal sentence). *Ula'ika* (those) is a second *mubtada'*, and *sharrun* (worse) is the *khabar* (predicate) of *ula'ika*. The whole phrase *ula'ika ma'a sharrun* is the *khabar* (predicate) of *alladhina*. Alternatively, the estimated reading is *hum alladhina* (they are those who), or *a'ni alladhina* (I mean those who). *Ula'ika* is then a *mustani'af* (a resumptive sentence, introduced as a new clause).

﴿Place (*makanan*)﴾: that is, rank (*makanah*) and station (*manzilah*), or dwelling (*maskanan*) and abode (*manzilan*).

﴿And further astray in way (*wa-adallu sabilan*)﴾: that is, more mistaken in path. This is *al-isnad al-majazi* (metaphorical attribution), and the meaning is: what drives you to these questions is that you stray from his way and despise his place and station. Had you looked with an eye of fairness, while you are among those who will be dragged upon their faces to Hell, you would know that your place is worse than his place, and your way is more astray than his way.

Within this same line of argument is His saying:

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God? Those whom God has cursed and with whom He is angry...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], to the end of the verse.

It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three categories: a category upon mounts, a category upon their feet, and a category upon their faces." It was said: "O Messenger of God, how will they walk upon their faces?" He (ﷺ) said: "The One who made them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 35:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾ — the Tawrah (Torah) — just as We gave you the Qur'an. ﴿And We appointed with him his brother Harun﴾ — (Harun is) a substitute (badal) or an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan). ﴿As a minister (wazir)﴾ — linguistically, it is one to whom one returns (for support) from the wazar, and wazar means refuge. The role of wazir does not contradict prophethood, for prophets were sent in one era, and they were commanded that some of them should support one another.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 36:

﴿So We said: "Go to the people who denied Our signs"﴾ — that is, to Pharaoh and his people. Its implied meaning is: so they went to them and warned them, but they denied them. ﴿Then We utterly destroyed them with destruction﴾. Al-tadmir (utter destruction) means annihilation by a wondrous manner. He intended to abbreviate the narrative, so he mentioned its beginning and its end, because these are the intended purpose of the story, namely the establishment of proof through the sending of the messengers and the deserving of destruction through their denial.

And the people of Noah — meaning: We destroyed the people of Noah when they denied the Messengers, i.e., Noah, Idris and Shith, peace be upon them; or their denial of one of them was a denial of all of them. ﴿We drowned them﴾ by the flood, ﴿and We made them﴾ — and We made their drowning, or (p-538) their story, ﴿a sign for mankind﴾, a lesson by which they take heed. ﴿And We have prepared﴾ and readied ﴿for the wrongdoers﴾ — the people of Noah. The original wording is "and We prepared for them," but he intended to describe them as wrongdoers, so he made it apparent. Or it is general for everyone who commits the wrong of shirk, and it includes them by its generality — ﴿a painful punishment﴾, namely the Fire.

ﷺ

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 38:**

﴿And ʿĀd﴾: We destroyed ʿĀd. ﴿And Thamūd﴾: Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ read it as Thamūd (without tanwīn) according to the interpretation of the tribe, while the others read Thamūdan (with tanwīn) according to the interpretation of the clan (ḥayy). Or it is because it is the name of the greatest forefather. ﴿And the companions of the Rass﴾: They are the people of Shuʿayb. They used to worship idols, so they denied Shuʿayb. While they were around the Rass, which is the unlined well, it collapsed upon them, and they and their dwellings were swallowed up by the earth. It is also said that al-Rass is a town whose people killed their prophet, so they were destroyed; or they are the companions of the trench (al-Ukhdūd), and al-Rass means al-Ukhdūd. ﴿And generations﴾: and We destroyed nations ﴿between that﴾ mentioned ﴿many﴾, whose number none knows except Allah. He sent messengers to them, they denied them, and so they were destroyed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 39:

﴿And each We struck with examples﴾: We made clear to him the wondrous stories from the stories of the earlier peoples. ﴿And each We utterly destroyed with total destruction﴾: That is, We destroyed with destruction, and "each" (kullan) is the first (object). The first (kullan) is in the accusative governed by what is implied by "We struck with examples for him," which is "We warned" or "We admonished." The second (kullan) is governed by "tabbarna" (We destroyed), because it is free for it (i.e., the verb has no other object to take, so it governs the second "kullan").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 40:

﴿And indeed they have passed by﴾, meaning: the people of Makkah, ﴿upon the town﴾, Sodom (Sadum), which was the greatest of the towns of the people of Lut, and they were five, of which God destroyed four along with their inhabitants, and one remained, ﴿which was rained upon with a rain of evil﴾, meaning: God rained stones upon it. That is, the Quraysh passed many times on their trade journeys to Syria over that town which was destroyed by stones from the sky. And ﴿a rain of evil﴾ is the second object, and the original is "the town was rained upon with a rain," or it is a verbal noun with its augmentations removed, meaning: "the raining of evil" (imtar al-su'). ﴿Did they not then see it?﴾ Did they not witness that with their own eyes during their journey to Syria, so that they would reflect and believe? ﴿Rather, they did not expect a resurrection﴾. Rather, they were a people who disbelieved in the resurrection and did not fear being raised, so they did not believe; or (p-539) they did not hope for a resurrection as the believers hope for it, due to their eagerness to attain the reward of their deeds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 41:

﴿And when they see you, they take you not except in mockery﴾. ﴿In⁠⁠﴾ is negative (in naafiyah, "not"). ﴿Except mockery﴾ (huzuwan): he took it as huzu'an, in the sense of "he mocked at it." The original form is "he took it in the place of mockery" (huzu'), or "one mocked at." ﴿"Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?"﴾ The phrase is reported after an implied verb of saying, and "this" (hadha) expresses belittlement and mockery; that is, they were saying, "Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?" The omitted element is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the returning pronoun referring to "the one" (alladhi) is omitted, that is, "whom God has sent (ba'athahu)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 42:

﴿Indeed, he nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them.﴾ *An* here is the lightened form (*mukhaffafah*) of *an-naqilah* (*inna*), and the *lam* is the *lam* that distinguishes (*lam al-fariqah*, the *lam* that separates the negated from the affirmed). This is evidence of the great effort (*mujahadah*) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in calling them to faith and in presenting the miracles to them, to the point that they, by their own claim, came close to abandoning their religion for the religion of Islam, had it not been for the extreme obstinacy (*lajaj*) and their clinging to the worship of their gods.

﴿And they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in way.﴾ This is a warning (*wa'id*) and an indication that they will not escape it, however long the period of respite (*imhal*) may be.

﴿Who is further astray in way?﴾ This serves as a response to their saying ﴿he nearly led us astray﴾, because it attributes to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being astray, since one cannot lead others astray except one who is himself astray.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 43:

﴿Have you seen him who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ That is: whoever obeys his desire in what he does and what he abandons, he is a worshipper of his desire, making it his god. So Allah the Exalted says to His Messenger: "This one who sees no object of worship but his desire, how can you hope to guide him to the right path?"

It is related that a man among the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to worship a stone; whenever he passed by a stone better than it, he would abandon the first and worship the second. And it is related from al-Hasan (al-Basri) that this refers to everyone who follows his desire in all things. ﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ That is: a protector who keeps him from following his desire and worshipping what he desires. Would you then be a trustee over him, so that you could turn him from desire to guidance? He (Allah) informed him that his duty is only to convey the message. (p-540)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 44:

﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like livestock; rather, they are even further astray in way.﴾

"Am" here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and its meaning is: "Rather, do you think that this blame is greater than the earlier one, to the point that it was made necessary to turn away from that and move on to this, namely that they have been deprived of hearing and understanding? For they do not lend an ear to listening to the truth, nor do they apply their minds to reflecting upon it, and they are likened to livestock, which are a proverb for heedlessness and misguidance. Satan has mounted them by making them submissive, because they abandoned reasoning. Then they are even more misguided than livestock, because livestock glorify their Lord, prostrate to Him, obey whoever feeds them, recognize who does good to them from who does them harm, seek what benefits them, avoid what harms them, and find their way to their pastures and watering places. These people do not submit to their Lord, do not recognize His kindness toward them over the harm of Satan, who is their enemy, do not seek the reward, which is the greatest of benefits, do not fear the punishment, which is the greatest of harms and destructions, and do not find their way to the truth, which is the wholesome spring and the sweet, refreshing water." 

They said: the angels have intellect and spirit, the beasts have soul and desire, and the human being is a combination of all of them as a test. If the soul and desire overcome him, he becomes lower than the livestock; and if the spirit and intellect overcome him, he surpasses the noble angels. "Most" is mentioned only because among them are those whom nothing has prevented from accepting Islam except love of leadership, and that is a stubborn disease; and because among them are those who did believe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 45:

﴿Have you not considered your Lord﴾: Have you not looked at the handiwork and power of your Lord? ﴿how He extends the shadow﴾: that is, He spreads it so that it covers the earth. This lasts from the break of dawn until the time the sun rises, according to the majority of scholars (al-Jumhur), because it is an extended shade with no sun in it and no darkness, just as He said of the shade of Paradise: ﴿and extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30], with no sun in it and no darkness. ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾: that is, permanent, never disappearing and not removed by the sun. ﴿Then We made the sun over it﴾: over the shade, ﴿an indicator﴾, because the shade is recognized through the sun, and were it not for the sun the shade would not be recognized, for things are known by their opposites.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 46:

﴿Then We withdrew it﴾, i.e., We took that extended shade ﴿to Us﴾, to wherever We willed, ﴿a gentle withdrawal﴾, easy and not difficult, or little by little, i.e., part by part, by means of the sun that comes upon it. He used ﴿thumma﴾ (then) to indicate the difference between the matters, as if the second is greater than the first and the third is greater than the second. The distance between them in excellence was likened to the distance between events in time.

﴿And He it is who made the night a garment for you﴾. He made the darkness, which covers, like a garment. ﴿And sleep a rest﴾: a rest for your bodies and a cutting-off of your activities. The root *s-b-t* means cutting off, and the sleeper is *masbut* (one whose activity has been cut off), because his action and movement have ceased. It has also been said that *subat* (deep sleep, rest) means death, and *masbut* means dead, because his life has been cut off. This is like His saying, ﴿And He it is who takes you back [in death] by night﴾ (Al-An'am: 60). This is supported by the mention of resurrection (*nushur*) in contrast to it: ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾. *Nushur* means rising up from sleep, like the resurrection of the dead, or it means that people are dispersed during it to seek their livelihood. This verse, along with its indication of the power of the Creator, is also a manifestation of His blessing upon His creation, because there are religious and worldly benefits in being concealed by the cover of the night. In sleep and waking, which are compared to death and life, there is a lesson for whoever takes heed. Luqman said to his son: "Just as you sleep and are awakened, so you will die and be raised."

﴿And He it is who sends the winds﴾. Al-Rih (الرِيحَ, "the wind"): this is a Meccan reading, and the noun is meant generically. ﴿as heralds of good news﴾: bushran (بُشْرًا) is a lightened form of bushur (بُشُرٍ), the plural of bashir (بشور). ﴿before His mercy﴾: that is, before the rain. The wind comes first, then the clouds, then the rain. This is an elegant metaphor (isti'arah, a figure in which one thing is described by the name of another).

﴿And We send down from the sky water﴾: rain. ﴿pure﴾ (tahuran, طَهُورًا): intensively pure in its purity. The word tahur is used as an adjective, as in your saying "māʾun ṭahūrun" (pure water), meaning ṭāhir (pure). It is also used as a noun for what is used for purification, like wuḍūʾ (ablution water) and wuqūd (fuel, for what is used to kindle fire). It is also a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the meaning of purifying, as in your saying "tatahhartu ṭahūran ḥasanan" (I purified myself with a good purification). From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no prayer except with ṭahūr", meaning with purification. What is reported from Tha'lab is that it is what is pure in itself and purifies others, which is the position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. If this is an additional clarification of its purity, then it is good. It is supported by the words of Allah, ﴿and He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it﴾ [al-Anfal: 11]. But if not, then fa'ul (فَعَوْلٌ) has nothing to do with taf'il (the intensive verb form), and analogizing it to what derives from transitive verbs, such as qatul (قَطُوعٌ) and manu' (مَنُوعٌ), is not sound. This is because the pattern of the passive participle is for intensification. If the verb is transitive, the derived form is transitive, and if it is intransitive, the derived form is intransitive.

﴿لِنُحْيِيَ بِهِ﴾ by the rain, ﴿بَلْدَةً مَيْتًا﴾ "a dead land." He used the masculine form *maytan* on the understanding that the noun means "the land" or "the place."

﴿وَنُسْقِيَهُ مِمّا خَلَقْنا أنْعامًا وأناسِيَّ كَثِيرًا﴾ means: We give the water to drink to the beasts and to people. "Of what We created" is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) modifying ﴿أنْعامًا وأناسِيَّ﴾, meaning: cattle and people, of what We created.

*Saqā* and *asqā* are two forms of the verb meaning "to give to drink." Al-Mufaddal and al-Barjamī read "وَنَسْقِيَهُ" (with the verb in the form of *asqā*).

*Al-anāsī* is the plural of *insī* by analogy, like *kursī* and *karāsī*, or it is the plural of *insān*. Its original form was *anāsīn*, like *saraḥān* and *sarāḥīn*. Then the *nūn* was changed to *yā'* and assimilated.

The giving of life to the earth is mentioned before the watering of cattle and people, because the earth's life is the cause of theirs. Cattle are singled out among drinking animals because most of people's benefits depend on them, so the favour of watering cattle is like the favour of watering people.

The word *baldah* is indefinite because He means some of the lands of those who are far from the places where water is expected.

Since watering people is among the purposes for which water was sent down, He described it as *ṭahūr* (purifying) as an honour to them, and to make clear that it is their duty to seek purity in their inner and outer selves, because *ṭahūriyya* (the quality of purifying) is a condition for the giving of life.

And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may take heed. [Qur'an 25:50]

**"لِيَذْكُرُوا" (liyadhkurū, "that they may remember")** is read by Hamzah and Ali. The meaning is: We have distributed this statement among people, in the Qur'an and in the rest of the books revealed to the messengers. It is the mention of the formation of clouds and the sending down of rain, so that they may reflect, draw lessons, recognise the true value of the blessing in it, and give thanks.

﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief.﴾ Most of them refused, except to deny the blessing, reject it, and pay it little attention.

Or it means: We distributed the rain among them across different lands, at different times, and in different forms: heavy rain (**wābil**), light drizzle (**ṭall**), abundant rain (**jawd**), fine mist (**radhādh**), and steady rain (**dīmah**). But they refused except to disbelieve, and to say, "We have been given rain by such-and-such a star-rising (**nawʾ**)," and they did not mention the making of Allah, the Exalted, and His mercy.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "There is no year with less rain than another, but Allah distributes it wherever He wills," and he recited the verse.

It is also reported that the angels know the number and quantity of the rain each year, because it does not vary, but what varies is the lands that receive it. From this is derived an answer concerning the indefinite forms used for "town" (**baldah**), "livestock" (**anʿām**), and "people" (**anāsī**) in the verse.

Whoever attributes rain to the star-risings and denies that the rain and the star-risings are both part of the creation of Allah, the Exalted, has disbelieved. But whoever holds that Allah, the Exalted, is the Creator of them, and that He has set the star-risings as signs and indications of them, has not disbelieved.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verses 51–52:

﴿And if We had willed, We would have raised in every town a warner.﴾ ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers.﴾ Meaning: if We had willed, We would have lightened for you the burdens of warning all the towns, and We would have raised in every town a prophet to warn it. But We willed to gather for you the virtues of all the messengers through the Message to the whole of mankind. So We confined the task to you and magnified you by it, and you are alone equal to them all. For this reason, you were addressed in the plural, "O messengers" (yā ayyuhā al-rusul). So meet that with thankfulness, patience and steadfastness, and do not obey the disbelievers in what they call you to, namely agreeing with them and flattering them (mudāhana). Just as I preferred you over all the prophets, prefer My pleasure over all desires. The purpose of this is to stir him up and to stir up and rouse the believers. ﴿And strive against them with it﴾: that is, with Allah, meaning with His help and His success; or with the Qur'an, meaning argue with them by it and rebuke them with their inability to match it. ﴿with a great striving﴾: a mighty striving, its station great before Allah because of the hardships it entails. It is also permissible for the pronoun in "with it" to refer to what is indicated by ﴿And if We had willed, We would have raised in every town a warner﴾, namely his being the warner of all the towns. For if a warner had been raised in every town, it would have been obligatory on every warner to strive against his own town, and so those striving efforts would have converged upon the Messenger of Allah. His striving therefore became great and mighty on that account. So He said to him: "And strive against them" by reason of your being the warner of all the towns, "with a great striving," comprehending every striving.

(p-544)
