Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 53:

﴿And it is He who let loose the two seas﴾: He left them side by side, adjacent to one another. One says "maraja al-dabbah" (مَرَجْتُ الدابَّةَ) when one lets the animal loose to graze. He called the two abundant, vast waters "two seas."

﴿This one﴾: i.e., one of them is ﴿sweet, fresh﴾. The word "furat" is an adjective of "adhb" (عَذْبٌ), meaning extremely sweet, to the point of approaching sweetness.

﴿And this one is salty, bitter﴾: the word "ujaj" is an adjective of "milh" (مِلْحٌ), meaning extremely salty.

﴿And He placed between them a barrier﴾: a partition from His power, which separates them and prevents them from mixing. Thus they are outwardly different, and in reality separate.

﴿And a forbidding restraint﴾: and a screen withheld from the eyes, like His saying ﴿a hidden veil﴾ [al-Isra: 45].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 54:

﴿And He it is Who created from water﴾ — that is, from the sperm-drop (nutfah) — ﴿a human being﴾, a person (basharan), ﴿and made him a lineage (nasab) and an affinity (sihr)﴾. He intended by this the division of humankind into two categories: those of lineage (dhawu nasab), that is, males to whom lineage is traced, so it is said "So-and-so son of So-and-so" and "So-and-so daughter of So-and-so"; and those of affinity (dhawat sihr), that is, females through whom affinity (musahara) is contracted, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So He made of him the two sexes, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. ﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾, in that He created from one sperm-drop a human being of two kinds, male and female.

It has also been said: ﴿and made him a lineage﴾, that is, kinship (qarabah), ﴿and affinity﴾, that is, marriage-relationship (musahara), meaning the bond through marriage, which belongs to the category of lineages, because connection is established through it and through affinity, since procreation takes place through both.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 55:

﴿And they worship besides Allah that which can neither benefit them﴾ if they worship it, ﴿nor harm them﴾ if they abandon it. ﴿And the disbeliever is ever an assistant﴾ against his Lord, that is, in disobedience to his Lord, ﴿ظَهِيرًا﴾ (ẓahīran), meaning a helper and one who supports. The form فَعِيل in the sense of مُفاعِل is not rare; ẓahīr and muẓāhir are like ʿawīn and mu'āwin, and al-muẓāhara means al-mu'āwana (mutual aid). The meaning is: the disbeliever, by worshipping the idol, follows Satan and assists him in disobedience to the Most Merciful.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 56:**

﴿And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a bringer of good tidings﴾ to the believers ﴿and a warner﴾ to the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 57:

﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it﴾, i.e., for the conveying (al-tabligh), ﴿any wage (ajr)﴾, meaning a reward (ju'l) of its kind, ﴿except that whoever wills may take a way to his Lord﴾ (p-545). The meaning is: except the doing of whoever wills, and its being an exception from the wage is like the saying of one who is compassionate toward you and has striven for you in acquiring wealth: "I do not ask from you any reward for what I have striven, except that you preserve this wealth and do not waste it." Your preserving your wealth for yourself is not of the same kind as a reward, but he has formed it in the form of a reward, as if he says: "Your preserving your wealth is in the position of a reward to me, and my contentment with it is like the contentment of one who is rewarded with a reward." By my life, indeed he (peace be upon him) was in this same regard with his community. The meaning of their taking a way to God is their drawing near to Him through faith and obedience, or through charity and spending. It was also said: the meaning is, "but whoever wills to take, by spending, a way to the pleasure of his Lord, let him do so." It was also said: its sense is, "I do not ask you any wage for what I call you to, except that the one called takes a way to his Lord by obeying Him; that is my wage, because God rewards me for it."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 58:

﴿And put your trust in the Ever-Living, who does not die﴾. Take as your guardian the One who does not die, who will not leave you to one who dies in humiliation. That is, trust in Him, and entrust your affair to Him to suffice you against their evils, and do not rely upon a living being who will die. Some of the righteous (al-salihin) recited it and said: "It is not proper for a person of intellect to trust in a created being after this." Tawakkul (complete trust, reliance) is: depending upon Him in every matter.

﴿And glorify Him﴾: exalt Him above leaving to others the one who has relied upon Him. ﴿With His praise﴾: with His grace, which necessitates praise. Or, say: "Glory be to Allah and with His praise." Or, exalt Him above all defects with a praise by which you extol Him.

﴿And sufficient is He as one who is aware of the sins of His servants﴾: that is, Allah is sufficient as One who is aware of the sins of His servants, meaning: He is Aware of their conditions and sufficient in recompensing their deeds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 59:

﴿Who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ That is, within a span of time whose measure is this period, because at that time there was no night and day. It is narrated from Mujahid that its first (day) was Sunday and its last was Friday. He created them in six days, though He is able to create them in an instant, as a lesson to His creation in gentleness (al-rifq) and deliberation (al-tathabbut). ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne, the Most Merciful﴾ That is, He is the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). Al-Rahman is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), or it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "istawa" (established), (p-546) or (it is) "alladhi khalaqa" (the one who created) as the subject (mubtada'), and "al-Rahman" its predicate. ﴿Then ask﴾ without a hamza (read so by Makki and Ali) ﴿about Him﴾ is the complement (silah) of "sal" (ask). It is like His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will befall﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1], just as it can be a complement in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you will be asked that Day about the delight﴾ [al-Takathur: 8]. So "sa'ala bihi" is like "ihtamma bihi" (be concerned with it) and "ishtaghala bihi" (be occupied with it), and "sa'ala 'anhu" is like your saying "bahatha 'anhu" (investigated it) and "fattasha 'anhu" (searched into it). Or the complement is "khabiran" [al-Furqan: 58], and "khabiran" is the object of "sal," meaning: ask about Him a knowledgeable man who will inform you of His mercy. Or: ask a man who is well-informed about Him and His mercy. Or "al-Rahman" is one of the names of God Most High mentioned in the earlier scriptures, which they did not recognize, so it was said: ask about this name whoever among the People of the Book will inform you, until you know who denies it. Hence they used to say: "We do not know al-Rahman except the one in al-Yamama," meaning Musaylima, who was called "Rahman al-Yamama."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 60:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ i.e., when Muhammad (ﷺ) says to the polytheists, ﴿Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., pray to God and humble yourselves before Him, ﴿they say: "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ i.e., "We do not know the Most Merciful so as to prostrate to Him." This is a question about the one named by it, because they did not know Him by this name, and the question is about something unknown, either "what" or about its meaning, because it was not in use in their speech as ar-Rahim (the Especially Merciful), ar-Rahim (the Merciful) and ar-Rahum (the Very Merciful) were in use. ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ i.e., to the One you command us to prostrate to, or to your command to prostrate, O Muhammad, without any knowledge on our part of Him. "Ya'muruna" (you command us) is read by ʿAli and Hamza, as if some of them said to others: "Shall we prostrate to what Muhammad commands us, or to what the One named Ar-Rahman commands us, whom we do not know what He is?" Thus they were obstinate, because its meaning, according to the people of the language (ahl al-lughah), is "the One possessing a mercy beyond which there is no further degree of mercy," since fa'lan (fa'lan) is among the patterns of intensification (ibniyat al-mubalaghah): you say "rajul ʿaṭshan" (a man extremely thirsty) when he is at the extreme of thirst. ﴿And it increased them﴾ in his saying "Prostrate to the Most Merciful" ﴿in aversion (nufuran)﴾, i.e., distance from faith.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 25, verse 61:

﴿Blessed is He who placed constellations in the sky﴾. The *burūj* (zodiacal constellations) are the stations (*manāzil*) of the wandering stars (planets). Each planet has two houses in which its condition becomes strong. The sun has one house and the moon has one house. So Aries (*al-Ḥamal*) and Scorpio (*al-ʿAqrab*) are the two houses of Mars; Taurus (*al-Thawr*) and Libra (*al-Mīzān*) are the two houses of Venus; Gemini (*al-Jawzāʾ*) and Virgo (*al-Sunbula*) are the two houses of Mercury (*ʿUṭārid*); Cancer (*al-Saraṭān*) is the house of the moon; Leo (*al-Asad*) is the house of the sun; Sagittarius (*al-Qaws*) and Pisces (*al-Ḥūt*) are the two houses of Jupiter (*al-Mushtarī*); and Capricorn (*al-Jady*) and Aquarius (*al-Dalw*) are the two houses of Saturn (*Zuḥal*). These constellations are divided among the four natures (*ṭabāʾiʿ*, the four elements), so that each of the four receives three constellations. Aries, Leo and Sagittarius form the fire triplicity (*muthallatha nāriyya*). Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn form the earth triplicity (*muthallatha arḍiyya*). Gemini, Libra and Aquarius form the air triplicity (*muthallatha hawāʾiyya*). Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces form the water triplicity (*muthallatha māʾiyya*). The stations are called *burūj*, which are the lofty palaces, because for these planets they are like dwellings for their inhabitants. The derivation of *burūj* is from *tabarruj* (displaying oneself), because of its visibility. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and Mujāhid said: the *burūj* are the large stars, because of their prominence.

﴿And He placed in it﴾, in the sky, ﴿a lamp﴾, meaning the sun, because of its blazing. Ḥamza and ʿAlī read *"surujan"* (سُرُجًا), i.e., stars. ﴿And a shining moon﴾, illuminating at night.

Verse 62: "And it is He who made the night and the day succeed one another (khilfah) for whoever wishes to take heed or wishes to be thankful."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 62:

﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي جَعَلَ اللَيْلَ والنَهارَ خِلْفَةً﴾ "Khilfah" is a form of the verb "khalafa" (to succeed, to follow), in the pattern "fi'lah," like "rikbah" from "rakiba" (to ride). It is the state in which the night and the day succeed one another, each of them taking the place of the other. The meaning is: He made them both possessed of succession, such that one of them follows the other when the other passes away, or follows it in making up what has been missed of one's wird (regular portion of worship).

﴿لِمَن أرادَ أنْ يَذَّكَّرَ﴾ "For whoever wishes to take heed," that is, he contemplates their subjugation (to the divine order) and their alternation, so that he comes to know their Governor (mudabbir).

"Yadhdhakkaru" (with the letters dhal and kaf both read with a shaddah on the dhal, a form of the verb with tashdid): Hamzah and Khalaf read it this way. That is, he remembers Allah, or what he has forgotten, and then makes it up.

﴿أوْ أرادَ شُكُورًا﴾ That is, he gives thanks for the blessing of his Lord upon him in them both.

"And the servants of the Most Merciful" is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is "those who walk," or the predicate is "those, they shall be rewarded." "Those who walk" and what follows it are a description (sifah). The attribution to "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) is for specification and distinction. He described His friends after describing His enemies.

"Upon the earth humbly" (﴿عَلى الأرْضِ هَوْنًا﴾) is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a description of the walking, meaning: humble ones, or walking humbly. Al-Hawn means gentleness and softness. That is, they walk with tranquility, dignity and humility, without exuberance, arrogance or haughtiness. So they do not stamp their feet or slap their sandals (in pride and insolence). For this reason some scholars disliked riding in the markets, and because of His words, ﴿وَيَمْشُونَ في الأسْواقِ﴾ [al-Furqan: 20].

"And when the ignorant address them" means the foolish, with what they dislike, "they say: Peace" (﴿قالُوا سَلامًا﴾), meaning a sound word, by which they remain safe from harm and falsehood. Or it means a greeting of withdrawal from you: we will not oppose you or act ignorantly toward you; so "peace" stands in place of "withdrawal." It was said that this was abrogated by the verse of fighting, but there is no need for that, for overlooking the foolish is commendable both in the Sharia and in good manners.

This is the description of their days. Then He described their nights with His words:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 64:

﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾. Sujjadan is the plural of sajid (one who prostrates), and qiyaman is the plural of qa'im (one who stands). Al-baytutah (spending the night) is the opposite of al-zuhur (being in the day), and it means that the night overtakes you, whether you sleep or do not sleep. They said: whoever recites anything of the Qur'an in prayer, even a little, has spent the night as one prostrating and standing. It is also said that the two are the two rak'ahs after maghrib and the two rak'ahs after 'isha'. The apparent meaning is that it is a description of them as those who enliven the night, or most of it.

And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever-binding."

*Ghuram* means a ruin that is inescapable. From the same root comes *al-gharim* (the debtor), because he is constantly bound to his debt.

He described them as those who enliven the night in worship, prostrating and standing, and then followed this with mention of their supplication. This indicates that, despite their diligence, they are fearful, earnestly imploring, and humbly entreating God to turn the punishment away from them.

Indeed, it (Hell) is evil as a dwelling-place and a station. That is, indeed Jahannam (Hell). "Sa'at" (evil is) is in the sense of "bi'sat" (evil is). In it there is an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) which is explained by "mustaqarran" (as a dwelling-place), and the object of blame (al-makhsūs bil-dhamm) is omitted; its meaning is: "it is evil as a dwelling-place and a station, it." This pronoun is what links the sentence to the subject of "inna" and makes it its predicate (khabar). Or, in the sense of "ahzanat" (it saddened), with the pronoun of the subject of "inna" in it, and "mustaqarran" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz). It is valid that the two explanations be interlocking and synonymous, and that both be part of the speech of Allah the Exalted and a relating of their statement.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 67:

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾. They did not exceed the limit in spending, or they did not eat for indulgence, nor did they wear clothes for vanity and showing off. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they did not spend on acts of disobedience. So al-israf (extravagance, excess) is exceeding the proper measure. A man heard another man saying: "There is no good in extravagance." He said: "There is no extravagance in good." And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever withholds a right has been stingy, and whoever gives where there is no right has been extravagant."

﴿And they are not stingy﴾: with the ta' vowelled with a ḍammah, read by Kufa; with the ya' vowelled with a ḍammah and the ta' with a kasrah, read by Medina and Syria; and with the ya' vowelled with a fatḥah and the ta' with a kasrah, read by Mecca and Basra. Al-qatr, al-iqtar and al-taqtir mean restriction, which is the opposite of extravagance.

﴿And their spending was between that﴾, i.e., between excess and stinginess, ﴿a measure﴾, i.e., a balance between the two. Qawam means balance between two things. The two accusative words, i.e., ﴿between that, a measure﴾, are two predicates. He described them with moderation, which lies between excess and shortcoming, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded with the like of this: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 29], and the verse.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan asked ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz about his expenditure when he married his daughter to him, and he said: "The good deed is between the two bad ones." ʿAbd al-Malik understood that he meant what is in this verse. It has also been said: those were the companions of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him; they did not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor did they wear their clothes for beauty and adornment, but to satisfy hunger, cover nakedness, and ward off heat and cold. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is extravagance enough that a man desires something and eats it."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 68:

﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah﴾, i.e., they do not associate partners with Him, ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾, i.e., He has forbidden it, meaning: He has forbidden its killing, ﴿except by right﴾: by retaliation (qawad), or stoning (rajm), or apostasy (riddah), or polytheism (shirk), or spreading corruption in the land (sa'y fi al-ard bi al-fasad). The phrase "by right" is connected either to the omitted verb "kill" (qatl) or to "do not kill" (la yaqtulun) above it. ﴿And do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse (zina)﴾. The negation of these major sins (kaba'ir) from His righteous servants is an allusion to what their enemies among the Quraysh and others were upon, as if it were said: "And those whom Allah has purified from what you are upon." ﴿And whoever does that﴾, i.e., the aforementioned, ﴿will meet a penalty (athaman)﴾, meaning the recompense for sin.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 69:

﴿Yudā‘af﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿yalqa﴾, because the two are in one meaning: the multiplication of the punishment is the meeting with sins (luqiyy al-āthām), as in His statement (p. 550):

"Wherever you come to us, you will alight upon us in our abodes, and you will find firewood, thick and blazing, and a fire kindled."

Thus ﴿tulmim﴾ is apocopated (majzūm), because it carries the meaning of ﴿ta'tinā﴾ (you come to us), since coming (al-ityān) is alighting (al-ilmām).

"Yudā'af" (with the consonant doubled, plain form) is read by Makki, Yazid and Ya'qub; "yudā'if" (with active doubling) is read by the Shami reader; "yudā'af" (passive, with doubling) is read by Abu Bakr. It may be taken as a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) or as a circumstantial clause (hal).

The meaning of ﴿yuḍā'if lahu al-‘adhābu yawma al-qiyāmah﴾ is: he will be punished, as the days pass in the Hereafter, with punishment upon punishment. It has also been said: when the polytheist commits sins together with polytheism, he is punished for the polytheism and for the sins together, so the punishment is multiplied in proportion to the punishment for which he is being punished.

﴿Wa-yakhlud﴾ is apocopated by the same particle that apocopates ﴿yuḍā'af﴾, and is put in the nominative by the one who puts it in the nominative, because it is coordinated with it (ma‘tūf ‘alayhi). ﴿Fīhi﴾ means "in the punishment." "Fīhī" (with the vowel lengthened, ishbā') is read by Makki and Hafs. Hafs singled out the lengthening for this word for the sake of emphasis in the threat, and the Arabs lengthen for emphasis, although the basic form of the pronominal hā' is the lengthened one.

﴿Muhānan﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hāl), meaning: humiliated.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 70:

﴿Except for one who repents﴾ from polytheism. This is an exception from the genus (istithna' min al-jins) in the accusative position (fi mawdi' al-nasb). ﴿and believes﴾ in Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, ﴿and does righteous work﴾ after his repentance. ﴿For those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾. That is: He will grant them success in good conduct after their ugly conduct, or He will erase those (deeds) through repentance and establish in their place good deeds, namely faith and obedience. He did not intend by this that the very same evil deed becomes a good deed; rather, the meaning is what we have mentioned. "Yubaddilu" (is read) with a single letter (mukhaffafan, i.e., without the doubling of the ba'): al-Barjami. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, He expiates the evil deeds, ﴿Merciful﴾, He replaces them with good deeds.

ۚ﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, indeed he turns back to Allah with a [true] turning back.﴾ That is: whoever repents and fulfils repentance through righteous action, then he turns in this way to Allah, the Exalted, with a turning back that is pleasing to Him, expiating sins and securing reward.

﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾, that is, lying. It means they shun the gatherings of liars and the sittings of sinners and do not approach them, keeping themselves pure from mixing with evil and its people, because witnessing falsehood is a form of partnership in it. Likewise, gazing at what the Sharia has not permitted makes them partners of its doers in sins, because their presence and their looking is a sign of approval and a cause of its increase. In the admonitions of Jesus (peace be upon him): "Beware of sitting with sinners." Or the meaning is "they do not bear false witness," with an elided modifier. According to Qatada, the intended meaning is gatherings of falsehood. According to Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, it means they do not witness idle amusement and singing.

﴿And when they pass by vain talk﴾, that is, obscenity and everything that ought to be discarded and cast aside. The meaning is: when they pass by people engaged in vain talk and occupied with it, ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾, turning away and honouring themselves by avoiding being soiled by it, like His saying: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. According to al-Baqir (may Allah be pleased with him): when they mention the private parts, they refer to them by euphemism.

(p. 551)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 73:

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord﴾ — i.e., the Qur'an is recited to them or they are admonished with the Qur'an — ﴿do not fall down upon them deaf and blind﴾. This is not a negation of falling down; rather it is an affirmation of it and a negation of deafness and blindness. Its like is: "Zayd does not meet me greeting [me]" — it is a negation of the greeting, not of the meeting. The meaning is: when they are reminded of them, they fall down prostrating and weeping, hearing with attentive ears and seeing with watchful eyes, [attending] to what they have been commanded and forbidden, unlike the hypocrites and their like. Its proof is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And of those whom We guided and chose, when the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping﴾ [Maryam: 58].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 74:

﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses"﴾ min (مِن) here is for explanation (lil-bayan). It is as if it were said: "Grant us coolness of eyes (qurrata a'yun)," and then the coolness was specified and explained by His words, ﴿from among our spouses﴾ and ﴿our offspring﴾. Its meaning is that Allah makes them, for them, a coolness of eyes. This is from their saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning "you are a lion." Or min is for the starting point (li'l-ibtida'), with the sense: "Grant us, from their side, what our eyes are cooled by of obedience and righteousness." "And our offspring" (wa dhurriyyatina): Abu 'Amr and the Kufans other than Hafs read it in the singular, intending the collective noun (li-iradat al-jins); the others read "dhurriyyatina" in the plural. ﴿Coolness of eyes﴾ (qurrata a'yun) is indefinite because the indefiniteness of the qurrah (coolness) requires it: a genitive construction (mudaf) cannot be made indefinite except by making the genitive complement (mudaf ilayh) indefinite. It is as if he said: "Grant us from them (min-hum) joy and delight." The word "a'yun" is used in the plural of paucity (qillah) rather than "uyun," because the intended meaning is the eyes of the God-fearing, and they are few in comparison with the eyes of others. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba: 13]. It is also permissible to say, regarding the indefiniteness of a'yun, that these are specific eyes, namely the eyes of the God-fearing. The meaning is that they asked their Lord to grant them spouses and descendants who are workers for Allah the Exalted, by whom they are gladdened and in whom their eyes are cooled. It has been said: there is nothing more cooling to the eye of the believer than to see his wife and children obedient to Allah the Exalted. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it is the child when he is seen writing jurisprudence (fiqh). ﴿And make us leaders for the God-fearing﴾, that is: imams (a'immah) who are followed by us in religion. He suffices with the singular for its indication of the category (jins) and for the absence of ambiguity. Or the meaning is: make each one of us an imam. It has been said regarding this verse that it indicates that leadership in religion should be sought and desired.

**﴿Those will be recompensed with the lofty chamber﴾**, i.e., the chambers (al-ghurufat), which are the elevated mansions in Paradise. It is stated in the singular, restricting it to one representative of the category (al-jins); evidence for this is His saying: **﴿And they will be secure in the chambers﴾** [Saba larger: 37]. **﴿Because they were patient﴾**, i.e., because of their patience in acts of obedience, in abstaining from desires, in bearing the harm of the disbelievers, in striving against them, in enduring poverty, and in other things. **﴿And they will be met therein﴾**: "wayalqawna" (and they will be met) is read by Kufi readers other than Hafs. **﴿With greetings﴾** (tahiyyah), meaning a supplication for long life, **﴿and peace﴾** (salam), meaning a supplication for safety. That is, the angels will greet them and salute them, or some of them will greet one another and salute one another.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 76:

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿How excellent it is as a dwelling-place and station﴾ — that is, the chamber (al-ghurfah) is an excellent place of settling (mustaqarr) and residence (muqām), a place of abode and dwelling. This is in contrast to ﴿Evil it is as a dwelling-place and station﴾ [al-Furqan: 66].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 25, verse 77:

﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication.﴾ "Ma" (what) here is interrogative in meaning, and it is in the accusative position. Its meaning: "What would my Lord do with you were it not for His calling you to Islam?" Or: "Were it not for your worship of Him," that is, He created you for His worship, as in His words ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. That is, what weight would your worship carry with your Lord? Or: "What would He do with your punishment were it not for your calling upon others with Him as gods?" This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful?﴾ [al-Nisa: 147]. ﴿So you have denied﴾ My messenger, O people of Makkah, ﴿so the punishment will be﴾ ﴿inevitable (lizaman)﴾, that is: possessing inevitability, or constantly adhering. The verbal noun of "lazama" was put in the place of the active participle. Al-Dahhak said: ﴿ma ya'bau﴾ means "He does not care for your forgiveness were it not for your calling upon another god along with Him."
